column2: Early the next morning, someone knocked. Miaozhu woke with a start. “Is that A’jin? What is it?” “Yes, it’s me,” A’jin called. “Mr Gu is here. He says he has urgent business to discuss with Master Hu.” Miaozhu shook Hu awake and told him. He threw on a robe, rose, and opened the door. Gu greeted him apologetically. “Forgive me for disturbing your pleasant dreams. There is news I must tell you at once.” Still sleepy, Hu collected himself. “What news? Not good, I suppose. Come in and sit down.” “No need. I shall come straight to the point. Brother Five has sent a special messenger. There may be trouble over the deal with the foreign merchant in Shanghai. Pang Er’s manager has been up to something...” “The fellow named Zhu?” Hu interrupted. “Yes. Zhu Guanzong, the man they call Pigsy.” “I could see from the start that he would be difficult.” Hu shook his head. “What has he done?” “The man Brother Five sent is very capable and explained everything in detail. This is what happened...”

Pigsy was fiercely ambitious. He wanted to use Pang Er’s resources to become the leader of the Jiangsu and Zhejiang silk merchants in Shanghai’s foreign settlement. Outwardly, out of consideration for his employer, he had to accommodate Hu; in secret, he had long been plotting to bring him down. Once Gu negotiated the sale to the foreign merchant, Pang’s prior instructions obliged Pigsy to follow suit. Unfortunately, Hu was away from Shanghai and could not immediately sign the contract. Gu’s departure for Tongli created a further opening. According to You Laowu’s information, Pigsy was preparing to betray Hu. He had already approached the foreign merchant and urged him to negotiate through himself instead. He too was willing to guarantee by contract that the merchant could buy all their silk for the next three years, while offering the present stock below Hu’s price. “This is what the fellow told him: ‘You needn’t worry that Hu will refuse to sell if you force down the price. You don’t know his real resources; I do. He is an empty shell. His capital has all been brought in from elsewhere. While it lies tied up in stock, he has to pay short-term interest. How can that calculation work? Never mind that he would still make a profit at a lower price—even if there were no profit, he would be thankful merely to recover his capital. Besides, once the new silk comes onto the market, old stock is bound to fall in price and become harder to sell.’” Gu grew angrier as he spoke, raising his voice as though in an argument. “Tell me, isn’t that bastard Pigsy a traitor to his own people?” “There is no need to be angry. I have my own ways of dealing with traitors.” Entirely unhurried, Hu called, “Miaozhu! Ask A’jin to bring Mr Gu something to eat.”

“No, no! I couldn’t eat. I am full of anger already. Little Uncle, I see only one solution. You, or perhaps Third Master Liu, must hurry to Nanxun and ask Pang Er to intervene. Meanwhile I shall return to Shanghai and organize the small dealers against Pigsy.” “Pang Er is Sun Wukong, and certainly knows how to bring Pigsy to heel. But we have not yet reached the point of summoning the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. As for organizing the small dealers against him, even when beating a dog you must consider its master. We should have difficulty explaining that to Pang.” “Little Uncle!” Gu was genuinely anxious. “You consider friendship and face at every turn. Haven’t you noticed that the other man considers neither when dealing with you?” Hu thought for a moment, then smiled. “I have a plan. If Pigsy knows what is good for him, we can let the matter drop. If he does not, he will find himself like Pigsy looking in a mirror—no human being on either side. I shall make him unacceptable to everyone!” “Excellent! Tell me, Little Uncle.” “No hurry. Sit down first.” Hu drew him into the bridal chamber. Miaozhu had hastily finished dressing. One night had changed her status, and Gu greeted her with a smile. “Auntie, congratulations!” Blushing, she answered, “You are too kind. Please sit down, Mr Gu. What has made you angry? I could hear you raising your voice.” “He is not angry now,” Hu put in. “Bring us some tea quickly. I am desperately thirsty.” Miaozhu summoned A’jin and attended to Hu’s washing while arranging refreshments for the visitor. Hu had said he had a plan merely to reassure Gu. Only after leisurely finishing his wash did he actually devise one.

Over breakfast, Hu explained his secret plan for dealing with Pigsy. Gu grasped it thoroughly and repeatedly expressed his agreement. As soon as they had settled everything, he left for Shanghai to carry it out. Following the agreed sequence, he first called on the foreign merchant. Gilbert, the head of Jardine Matheson, was an Englishman formerly employed by the East India Company, and a highly accomplished actor. The moment he saw Gu, he expressed regret that they had not signed a preliminary agreement when they first settled the sale. News had now arrived from Europe that silk prices had fallen, so the transaction could not proceed at the original price. He was personally very sorry. Had they signed a preliminary contract, he added, it would have had to be honored; even knowing that it would lose money, the head office could have done nothing about it. In short, Gu had only his own delay to blame. “Yes, failing to sign a preliminary agreement was my mistake. But Chinese merchants value good faith. Once we have given our word, it is as binding as a written contract.” Gu asked calmly, “We have no means of verifying whether silk prices in Europe have fallen. I want to ask only this: are you still willing to buy our silk at the agreed price?” “I am sorry. I have made myself quite clear,” Gilbert replied. “If you will reduce the price by fifteen percent, we can still do business.” “Impossible. You will have to pay our price, whichever Chinese merchant supplies your silk.”

The breakdown in negotiations was expected. Leaving Jardine Matheson, Gu went straight to Tongxing Bank on Second Road, produced a five-thousand-tael banknote, and deposited it in an account called Fuji. “Very good,” said the clerk. “May I have your passbook?” “I have no passbook. We are Yuji Silk Warehouse and have business dealings with Fuji. Accept the money and give me a receipt.” This was a customary business procedure. Tongxing issued a receipt stating, “Received from Yuji Silk Warehouse, for deposit to the account of Fuji, exactly five thousand taels of silver,” and handed it to Gu. It also notified Fuji of the deposit. Fuji was Pigsy’s account; his name was Zhu Funian. The notice from Tongxing astonished him, so it was the first thing he mentioned when Gu called. “My dear fellow, there are no payments due between us. Why have you put five thousand taels into my account?” “A small token from Mr Hu. He says we often put you to trouble and he has long wished to show his appreciation. Now that he has made a profit on silk, he must naturally send you a share.”

“You are too generous, too generous.” Zhu suddenly assumed an anxious expression. “Brother Yingchun, have you only just returned to Shanghai?” “Yes.” “Then have you met Mr Gilbert of Jardine Matheson?” “I have. That is precisely why I have come for your advice. Gilbert says silk prices have fallen in Europe and wants to force down our price. What should we do?” “Well... that has been worrying me too. These foreigners are dreadful. We must stand together against him. If he demands a reduction, we must refuse to sell.” “You have ample resources and can afford to wait. Our capital is small; we cannot.” “You are too modest.” Zhu probed further. “Are you anxious to dispose of your stock, Brother Yingchun?” Gu nodded, his expression grave and sincere. “To tell you the truth, before the sale was agreed, we could still have delayed payments elsewhere. But once it seemed certain, we promised everyone that their money would soon be settled. Now the cooked duck has flown away. We can only ask you to help us through this difficulty.” “I hardly deserve such confidence. My powers are limited, and I cannot decide on my own...” “Naturally, we would not put you in a difficult position,” Gu interrupted. “This will not be our last transaction with the foreigners. However hard things are, we cannot destroy our future. You know the trade and understand how formidable they are. Whatever happens, we will not sell this silk to them at a reduced price. I have already told Gilbert that whichever Chinese merchant he buys from, he must pay the agreed price. If we all stand together, he will have to yield. Here is my idea: keep the advantage on our own side. We can take a little less profit, while you gain something for helping us.”

Gu then explained his proposal. They would sell their silk to Zhu at ninety-five percent of the original price agreed with Gilbert. In other words, Zhu would receive a five-percent advantage, amounting to sixteen thousand taels. Gu appeared earnest, but was actually setting a trap. Had Zhu understood the situation, accepted the five-thousand-tael gift, and stopped obstructing them, all could have ended well. Gu would still represent the trade in negotiations with Gilbert, as originally arranged; the contract would be signed, the sale concluded, and everyone would share the benefits. But greed clouded Zhu’s judgment. With a wish-fulfilling scepter in one hand and an abacus in the other, so to speak, he reflected that a single resale would bring him more than ten thousand taels. By signing the contract himself, he would also immediately become the leader of the trade. How could he pass up such a chance to gain both money and standing? Delighted though he was, he had to maintain appearances. “Brother Yingchun, I shall do everything within my power. But I am working for another man. This can be done, though the rules require me to consult my employer first. May I give you an answer in three or four days?” Hu had anticipated this excuse. Gu laughed inwardly: one of the fellow’s feet was already caught, and he still knew nothing of the trap. Aloud he said, “Certainly. That is the proper procedure. But please give it your most urgent attention.”

“I understand. Within four days at most, you shall have a definite answer. As for those five thousand taels, I really cannot accept them. Please take them back.” Zhu reached for his keys to open the foreign-made safe and fetch banknotes. “No!” Gu stopped the hand holding the keys and lowered his voice. “Sooner or later, we have to pay it. Once we have a definite answer in four days, I shall make up the balance.” “Yes, yes...” Zhu had not quite understood. Gu spoke still more quietly. “How the discount is arranged and how the transaction is entered in the accounts is entirely up to you. If the sale is recorded at the original price, we shall pay another eleven thousand taels into Fuji.” This was an invitation to dishonesty. Zhu could tell Pang that, to help Hu, he had advanced the full original price agreed with Gilbert, entering that entire amount in the books while secretly receiving a sixteen-thousand-tael kickback. It was one possible method. Unable to decide immediately, Zhu naturally kept that option open. He nodded. “Very well. We can settle the account when the time comes.” They parted on excellent terms. Back at Yuji Silk Warehouse, Gu found You Laowu and burst into triumphant laughter before speaking a word.

Since arriving in Shanghai, Gu had been occupied with the foreign merchant and Pigsy. During their brief encounter, You had learned only that Hu had supplied an ingenious plan, without hearing its details. Gu’s delighted laughter therefore pleased but puzzled him, and he was eager for an explanation. Even after hearing the account, he still failed to understand. “What is the trick? I don’t see it. Four days from now, if you sell to Pigsy at your proposed price, you will simply hand him sixteen thousand taels and promote him to leader of the trade into the bargain.” “It will not be that easy for him. Wait until I have written a letter. As soon as Third Master Liu arrives, he will take it straight to Nanxun. Then Pigsy will find himself facing that mirror, with neither side willing to call him human!” “Ah!” You had been shown the way, but did not yet see it clearly. “Pang has a rich young gentleman’s pride and cares about appearances. His friendship with Little Uncle is sound too. But if Pigsy is making money for his employer, surely Pang cannot call that wrong?” “Can’t he? Brother Five, put yourself in Zhu’s place. How many courses are open to him?” You considered. “Three. He could trade privately on his own account, keeping any profit and charging any loss to his employer. That is the gravest offense an employee can commit. Second, he could follow your suggestion, tell Pang that he is helping you by advancing the full price, and secretly pocket the five-percent rebate. That would be falsifying the accounts and cheating his employer too. But if he honestly buys your silk for Pang at ninety-five percent of the price and enters the sixteen-thousand-tael gain in the business accounts, there is nothing wrong with it.”

“Quite right. Unfortunately for him, we have something else against him.” Gu flourished the receipt issued by Tongxing. “That?” You looked doubtful. “Can that count as evidence against him?” “Why not? It depends how the story is told.” Gu was thoroughly pleased with himself. “We need not say he used his employer’s power to extort money from us. We need only say that he took an outsider’s money to betray his employer: without paying him five thousand taels, we could never have obtained such a price for our silk.” “I understand!” You exclaimed. “You mean Gilbert offered eighty-five percent, but we conspired with Pigsy to raise it to ninety-five?” “Exactly! Why else would we have given him five thousand taels? Because we had so much money it was going moldy?” “That is a vicious bite. But what if he gives it back? Wouldn’t that clear him?” “How could it? If he had absolutely refused the money today and immediately told his employer, ‘They offered me five thousand taels, but I refused,’ he could stand his ground. He has missed that chance. The suspicion will not wash away.” You thought it over. Quite true! “Little Uncle can devise a poisonous scheme when he chooses,” he said with a laugh. “Of course, Pigsy has only his own greed to blame. Those five thousand taels began as ginseng fruit; now they are arsenic wrapped in sugar. I wonder when the poison will act.” “As soon as the letter arrives. It is a very important letter. I must begin at once.”

Gu composed it with great care, writing to Pang in Hu’s voice to ask for help. The first paragraph explained that Gilbert was demanding a lower price and that Hu, urgently needing to turn his stock into cash, had already spoken to Zhu. The second quoted Zhu’s own words and explained the reason for writing: Zhu had said that he dared not decide without his employer’s approval, so Hu was appealing directly to Pang, hoping that he would “extend your fullest assistance and relieve my pressing difficulty.” The third paragraph was hardest to frame. It had to convey regret within an expression of shame, and dissatisfaction within the regret. With Pang’s wholehearted support at the outset, Hu had expected to accomplish something by drawing on his resources. Instead, matters had reached this unfortunate pass. Naturally, Hu’s own inadequacy was to blame; he had disappointed a good friend’s generosity. That supplied the shame and regret. But why had matters reached such a pass? Because Pigsy had been interfering. This could not be stated outright, yet neither could it be too obscure. Between explicit statement and suggestion, the wording had to arouse just enough concern and suspicion in Pang to compel an inquiry. Too much or too little would spoil the effect. Fortunately, Gu’s Chinese was good as well as his English. He revised repeatedly and consulted You until the balance was exactly right. Once the letter had been copied and checked word by word, they had only to wait for Liu. You thought it must reach Nanxun as quickly as possible, whether Zhu truly intended to consult his employer or had some other purpose. They must get their version before Pang first. Gu agreed, but without Liu, the only available man who knew Pang, they could do nothing.

“Let us go to meet him. If we can intercept Third Master Liu at Songjiang and send his boat straight to Nanxun, we shall save at least a day.” “Very well,” Gu said. “I can wait for Seventh Sister at your house. Little Uncle may have arrived too. Whatever we need to discuss can be discussed in Songjiang just as well.” They left instructions at Yuji: if they missed Liu on the way and he reached Shanghai, he was to return to Songjiang immediately. In fact, You knew people everywhere along the water route and asked as they traveled, so there was little chance of missing him. Their arrival in Songjiang proved the wisdom of the move. They reached home early in the morning and found Liu in the sitting room, drinking his morning wine. He had arrived the previous evening, escorting the Seventh Lady and Furong to stay with the You family, and intended to leave by boat for Shanghai at noon. “Where is Little Uncle?” You asked. “He still has important business to discuss with Education Commissioner He. He should be back in Shanghai in a day or two.” “Never mind him for now,” Gu said. “Third Master, there is no time to lose. Take your wine aboard and drink it there.” “Certainly.” You arranged a boat while Gu explained the mission in detail, dwelling on every crucial point. His repeated warning was, “Be careful what you say. The more you talk, the more likely you are to make a mistake.” “Understood. Don’t worry. If anyone asks, I shall simply say I was in Tongli and know nothing about it.”

A Wuxi fast boat, its oarsmen working in shifts without stopping day or night, carried Liu to Nanxun. He hired a sedan chair on landing and went straight to the Pang residence. His timing was both unfortunate and fortunate. Unfortunate, because Pang’s mother was celebrating her sixtieth birthday; fortunate, because distinguished guests had gathered, and a companion of Liu’s talents was exactly what was needed. After Liu had kowtowed in the birthday hall, Pang caught him by the arm. “Third Brother Liu, you could not have come at a better time. I have some guests I need you to entertain.” Gamblers, naturally. Liu’s heart and hands both itched to begin, though the serious business must come first. This was the birthday itself. There had been a preliminary celebration the day before, and a further celebration would follow the next, making three days in all. Guests from afar, still eager for diversion, would doubtless gamble for several more days. Liu reckoned that he could not return to Shanghai for at least five days. Two days passed, and he had made many new friends. He worked hard, arranging games according to the guests’ tastes so that everyone was satisfied. They praised him freely, which reflected well on their host. Pang consequently took a great liking to him. On the third morning, before the gaming began, he came especially to the small reception pavilion where Liu was lodging to thank him for his trouble.

After expressing his thanks and exchanging a few remarks, Pang mentioned Hu. “Old Hu is wonderfully attentive to courtesy. He sent someone specially with gifts yesterday. I am deeply touched.” Liu was alert and answered gracefully. “It was only right. Had that silk not left him at his wits’ end, he would surely have come himself to kowtow and wish your mother a happy birthday, considering his friendship with you.” This reminded Pang of the business. Frowning, he said, “I have the greatest admiration for Hu’s skill at making the most of his resources. How could things have come to this? Nor do I understand how he fell out with the foreigners. According to Zhu Funian, he was too impatient and let them see the true extent of his resources, so they took the opportunity to put pressure on him. Is that what happened?” “I do not really know. A man named Gu handles all his dealings with the foreigners, so I know very little of that side.” “You mean Gu Yingchun? I know of him too. Extremely capable, and well trusted by the foreigners. With him, Hu is like a tiger given wings. That makes it still harder to understand.” The conversation was approaching the point Liu wanted. Secretly pleased, he continued to feign ignorance. “What is hard to understand?”

Quite unhurried, Liu said, “It is only right that I should help with your mother’s birthday. If you need me, I shall gladly stay eight or ten days. But Xueyan sent me here especially with a letter. May I ask you to read it first?” Pang opened it and glanced rapidly down the page. Before he had finished, he said repeatedly, “A small matter, a small matter! Zhu Funian is coming today too. I shall give him instructions.” The letter required leisurely reflection before its full meaning could emerge. In the present circumstances, Pang had no time to study it. Gu’s painstaking composition seemed to have become a coquettish glance thrown at a blind man. Bound by the warning against talking too much, Liu could say little, but he ought to inform Gu of this unexpected development so that Gu could prepare. Having decided, he assumed a delighted air. “With your help, I can give a satisfactory account of my mission. They are waiting for news in Shanghai. I shall write a letter and send my boat back with it, then return to help entertain your guests.” “Why trouble to go yourself? Where is the boat? Write the letter and I shall have someone take it.” “No need, no need. I had meant to return in the same boat. Since I must now stay another couple of days, I ought to collect my belongings from it. I had better go myself.” Pang could only let him. He provided a servant and a sedan chair to take Liu to the landing. Liu first packed his luggage aboard and sent it away under the Pang servant’s care. Then he wrote his letter in the cabin and instructed the boatman to return immediately to Songjiang and deliver it to You Laowu.

“What should have been a brilliant success has become this wretched muddle. That is what I cannot understand. With Hu’s skill and Gu’s, backed by Hu’s resources and mine, I cannot believe they would fail to get the better of the foreigners!” “Exactly!” Liu looked as though the thought had only just been suggested to him. Blinking and frowning, he said, “By rights, it should not have happened. When I return to Shanghai, I must ask him why.” “We shall go together,” Pang promptly offered. “I have wanted to go for some time, but could not leave because of my mother’s birthday. There are still a few guests to whom I owe particular attention. They will all leave tomorrow, so we could set out the day after.” An almanac happened to lie on the desk. Liu opened it and found the entry for the day after tomorrow. Beneath a large “Auspicious” was a dense row of small characters. Plainly it was a lucky day. There was a saying about almanacs: “A fool looks for the long entry.” Long entries listed the many activities favored that day. An unlucky “broken day” had only the short warning, “Nothing should be undertaken.” “The day after tomorrow favors travel,” Liu urged. “After that, there is no good day for another five days. I travel so often that it makes no difference to me, but you have not been away for some time. You ought to choose a lucky day.” Pang considered briefly, then decided. “Very well. We shall definitely leave the day after tomorrow.”

Liu attended to the guests while Pang prepared for the journey. A wealthy young gentleman cared about appearances: the gifts he meant to distribute filled half a boat. Besides Nanxun specialties, there were two chests of porcelain birthday bowls, specially commissioned at Jingdezhen to commemorate his mother’s sixtieth birthday. These were for relatives and friends who had sent gifts but had not attended. The end of the fifth lunar month was oppressively hot, and traveling was a misery. Pang had his own solution. They made the water journey at night, mooring by day beneath thick willow shade. There were two boats: one for the luggage and servants, the other a spacious passenger boat for Pang and Liu. Besides his personal attendants, Pang had brought a particularly clever young maid. Enjoying the cool, drinking tea and wine, and chatting, they passed the time very pleasantly. Along with women and gambling, they naturally discussed Hu. Pang was a pampered son of wealth, but he came from a business family. He was quite different from the heedless, arrogant young masters of official households. He understood trade and could distinguish good from bad and right from wrong. Liu, moreover, was careful at every turn. Whenever Hu’s present difficulty arose, he approached it obliquely, chiefly to awaken suspicion and curiosity. Pang was thus led to take out Gu’s letter and read it again. This time it made him deeply uneasy. During the birthday festivities, with guests crowding the house, he had had no leisure to think. When Zhu arrived, he had merely told him in haste to do as Hu requested. That had seemed right, but was actually wrong. Given his friendship with Hu, how could he take sixteen thousand taels from him by buying at a five-percent discount? Naturally, he ought to buy at the full price originally offered by the foreigner.

“Terrible, terrible!” Pang exclaimed in distress. “Hu must be cursing me for being a poor friend. Third Brother Liu, you must explain for me.” He told Liu how he had been careless. “Brother Pang, you worry too much. Hu is not that sort of man. He can scarcely thank you enough for helping him. Why should he take offense?” “What sort of help is that? To help him properly, I should...” Pang stopped abruptly, his mind filling with questions. The answer was plain. Helping Hu meant standing with him and forcing the foreign merchant to yield. Their friendship required it; their earlier agreement made it still more necessary. Yet they were plainly pursuing separate courses. Had Hu himself retreated before the difficulty and abandoned their agreement to stand together, or was there some other reason? Pang must find out. Like other pampered young gentlemen, once a question arose he wanted an immediate answer. He ordered the boatmen to travel all night and press on at full speed. On reaching Shanghai, he invited Liu to stay with him at the Yipinxiang Inn, then immediately sent his personal attendant, Pang Yi, to summon Zhu Funian. During the journey Liu had heard enough of Pang’s doubts to suspect that their meeting might bring a furious reprimand. As an outsider, he would be awkwardly placed between them. He therefore said that he must go and see Hu first. Pang did not insist on his staying, but asked him to bring Hu back afterward so that they could have a proper talk.

“Now Pigsy is in for it!” Having heard Liu’s account, Gu turned excitedly to Hu. “Let us proceed as planned!” They had established what Zhu was doing. He had originally intended to trade on his own account. But the celebration of Pang’s mother’s birthday had intervened. At Nanxun, Pang mentioned Hu’s letter first, and Zhu promptly changed his story, saying that this was precisely the matter on which he had come to ask the Second Young Master’s instructions. As You had foreseen, it had thus become a legitimate transaction to make money for his employer. Gu had made arrangements to meet this development. A lively, small-scale silk merchant from Nanxun knew Pang well and was also Gu’s good friend. Through him, Gu intended to disclose Hu’s secret dealings with Zhu to Pang. That private arrangement had already been brought to an end: the five thousand taels had been returned. With deliberate malice, Gu had issued a separate receipt to Zhu and kept Tongxing’s original document as evidence against him. Hu, however, no longer wished to pursue this course. “No need. Pang values friendship and is sure to give me some satisfaction. Besides, Zhu has learned his lesson. Why break his rice bowl? We had better take the proper course.” By the proper course, Hu meant drawing his friendship with Pang still closer. They decided to give him a welcoming dinner at Second Miss’s rooms in Yiqing House. Hu had meant to call at once and invite him personally, but the possibility that Pang was talking to Zhu made a visit inconvenient. He would send an invitation first. “There is someone else we should invite,” Gu said with a smile that suggested no good intentions. “You mean Zhu? Strictly speaking, we ought to. But I doubt he will come.” “Whether he comes or not, send it!”

The invitation sent to the Yipinxiang Inn brought back a basket of gifts: birthday bowls, local specialties, and a letter in which Pang thanked Hu and promised to arrive punctually. Dinner was set for six in the evening, but Pang came at half past five. After a cheerful exchange of greetings and recollections, Hu introduced You and Gu. Pang had long known Gu by reputation. Finding him a man of polished manners, fashionable clothes, and easy social presence increased his liking. As for You, hearing that he was a leading figure in the Grain Transport Brotherhood lent him an immediate air of mystery. His plain, awkward manner only sharpened Pang’s curiosity. Wealthy young gentlemen often enjoyed knowing men of the brotherhoods, and You seemed honest and approachable. They were soon as friendly as old acquaintances. Pang felt that accepting Hu’s invitation had brought him much. “Where is your Mr Zhu?” Hu asked. “Why did he not come with you?” At the mention of Zhu, Pang’s smile disappeared. His expression showed not only embarrassment but anger. “Old Hu,” he said after a pause, “we had better discuss this privately.” Turning to Second Miss, he asked, “Second Sister, is there a quiet room where we can talk?” “Certainly. This way, please.” She led them to the little room where You usually smoked opium. A smoking tray stood ready on the rosewood couch. As she lit the Taigu lamp, she asked, “Second Young Master Pang, would you like a pipe?” Pang enjoyed reclining by an opium tray but had no habit. With serious business to discuss, he had no inclination to smoke for amusement and shook his head. Knowing that their conversation was private, Second Miss withdrew quietly and closed the door.

“Old Hu,” Pang began in a strange, anxious voice, “what do you think of that man Zhu?” Hu considered briefly. “I do not know him well.” “Perhaps not, but you have had dealings with him. Those eyes of yours are like lightning. Nothing escapes them. We are good friends, and to tell you the truth, there are few men I admire. You must tell me everything you know, without holding anything back.” His sincerity moved Hu and also made him uneasy. Considering the words carefully, he felt that Pang must have developed grave suspicions of Zhu. Could it be...? “Has Zhu been making a mess of your affairs?” he could not help asking. “I cannot yet be certain.” Pang nodded. “I always thought him utterly loyal as well as capable. Now I find that things are not as I supposed.” “How so?” “It all began with your business. I wondered why matters had turned out this way when I had agreed to give you full authority to deal with the foreigners. So as soon as I arrived, I sent for Zhu and questioned him. The more I asked, the less satisfactory his answers became. It would take too long to explain everything. I felt that he hardly seemed to understand our friendship and had not cooperated with you. Old Hu,” he asked emphatically, “is that true?” Hu chose not to answer at once. After a deliberate hesitation, he said, “It is over. There is no need to discuss it further.”

“Then it is true! My suspicions were right. After that I asked about my own business.” Pang swallowed and continued with difficulty. “Once you begin to suspect someone, you find faults everywhere...” “That is not always so,” Hu interjected. “I am not wronging him. There really are faults.” “In the accounts?” “I have not examined the books yet, but I asked about a few transactions and already found things that made no sense. Take your affair. In Nanxun I told him to do as Mr Hu wished. When I asked today, he said that payment for the goods had not yet been sent to you. That is wrong.” “There is nothing wrong with it.” To behave generously, Hu had to defend Zhu. “Under the usual procedure, we should contact him first. We need to check our stock and establish the exact quantity before settling the account. That has caused the delay.” “No!” Pang shook his head vigorously. “Business rests on good faith. He knows our friendship. Once I had given those instructions, he should have sent the payment first; we could settle the precise account afterward. Instead, his conduct makes enemies of my friends—of my fellow merchants, you might say. What use have I for him?” His tone suggested that he meant to dismiss Zhu. That had originally been Hu’s intention, but now his thinking had changed. Pang had proved a true friend. Hu must consider Pang’s interests without allowing private motives to intrude, so he too shook his head.

“Brother Pang, if this alone has made you so angry, I cannot agree...” “There is more, of course,” Pang interrupted. “For example, a piece of land at Nicheng Bridge. He brought it to my attention, and we intended to buy it and build commercial premises to let. That was two months ago. I always assumed the purchase had been completed. Today, when I asked, he said that someone else had got there first. But when I asked who the buyer was, he could not tell me. Think of it, Hu: if he knew someone had bought it first, how could he not know the buyer’s name? Why had he not asked? I mean to investigate and see whether he has been playing some trick himself. There are many other contradictions in what he says. I trusted him before and overlooked them; now everything sounds wrong. I cannot keep employing this man. Don’t you agree?” Hu knew too little of Pang’s affairs to give a hasty judgment. Before answering, he asked, “Who is in overall charge on your side?” “He is! I trusted him so completely, and he has betrayed me. The man has no conscience!” Pang replied angrily. There was nothing unusual in this. Open and concealed fraud in the finances of wealthy households was commonplace: when the master fell, his retainers grew fat. Zhu appeared to be a ruthless man. Faced with an employer in Pang’s present mood, he might decide to go to extremes, and serious trouble could follow.
